title: Hot-route capacity protection — capacity risk model + demand forecast (working sheet)
content:
NOTE: This is a working spreadsheet-style doc captured as text. Numbers are directional (planning + sizing), not commitments.

Primary question this sheet answers:
- If top enterprise routes spike or misbehave (retry storm, client bug) OR we lose capacity (regional dip / perf regression), what reserved capacity buffers do we need to keep enterprise lane SLOs intact without fleet-wide impact?

Definitions (aligned w/ hot-route capacity protection program)
- “Hot route” = top enterprise endpoint+model combo that dominates traffic/cost and has contractual SLO sensitivity.
- “Enterprise lane” = priority routing lane in router (ENG-4824) with admission control + reserved headroom.
- “Self-serve lane” = default lane; can be throttled earlier during overload.
- “Capacity unit” = effective decode token throughput (tok/s) at target latency envelope (p95) for a given model class.
- Regions modeled: us-east-1, eu-west-1 (others later).

Assumptions (please challenge)
A1. Target enterprise lane protection goal (during overload):
- Keep enterprise availability >= 99.9% daily for top hot routes.
- Keep p95 latency degradation <= +25% vs baseline for chat routes during partial capacity loss.

A2. Baseline headroom (non-incident):
- Fleet runs ~70% utilization at peak (=> ~30% headroom) in each region for these model classes.
- When enterprise lane is enabled, reserved headroom is carved out from that 30% (i.e., it’s “untouchable” by self-serve during overload).

A3. Retry amplification during incidents:
- For 429/503 events, many clients retry. Observed retry amplification ranges 1.2x–2.5x depending on customer SDK behavior.
- For modeling, we use 1.8x on request rate for the impacted route for 15 minutes unless customer is known-good (exponential backoff + jitter).

A4. Throughput degradation modes:
- Regional capacity dip: -25% effective capacity (spot churn, AZ impairment, node health).
- Perf regression: -15% effective capacity for a model class (kernel regression, mis-tuned batching).
- Control-plane config propagation delay: 10–20 min inconsistent enforcement across regions (doesn’t reduce capacity, but increases thundering herd risk).

A5. Conversions / unit economics simplifications:
- For chat routes, we model capacity by decode tok/s and treat prefill as a latency penalty rather than a hard capacity cap (this is imperfect; runtime team says prefill saturation can dominate at large contexts — see open questions).
- Average tokens per request at peak derived from last 14d p50/p95 of prompt+completion tokens; we size against p95 tokens/req.

================================================================================
TAB: Inputs — “Top routes” list (initial)

Hot routes included (v0 list, from SRE + PM review; may change after PM-612 final):
1) route_id: chat_enterprise_general
   API: POST /v1/chat/completions
   Typical models: rw-llama-70b, rw-mixtral-8x22b (enterprise pinned)
2) route_id: chat_enterprise_longctx
   API: POST /v1/chat/completions (long context workloads)
   Typical models: rw-llama-70b-long (profile)
3) route_id: embeddings_enterprise
   API: POST /v1/embeddings
   Typical models: rw-embed-large
4) route_id: rerank_enterprise
   API: POST /v1/rerank
   Typical models: rw-rerank-v2

Traffic tiers (simplified for this sheet)
- Tier 0: Enterprise (contractual SLOs; priority lane)
- Tier 1: Pro / Pay-as-you-go (self-serve; higher limits)
- Tier 2: Free / trial (self-serve; lowest priority)

================================================================================
TAB: Baseline metrics (last 14d) — peak hour summaries

Units:
- RPS = requests/sec
- tok/req = total tokens per request (prompt+completion) at p95
- tok/s = RPS * tok/req

Table 1 — us-east-1 baseline (peak hour)
| route_id                   | tier  | baseline_RPS | p95_tok_per_req | baseline_tok_per_s | notes |
|---------------------------|-------|--------------|-----------------|--------------------|-------|
| chat_enterprise_general   | Ent   | 14.0         | 1650            | 23100              | mix of short+medium completions |
| chat_enterprise_longctx   | Ent   | 3.2          | 6200            | 19840              | fewer reqs, huge contexts |
| embeddings_enterprise     | Ent   | 52.0         | 420             | 21840              | stable; spiky at top-of-hour batch jobs |
| rerank_enterprise         | Ent   | 18.0         | 900             | 16200              | latency sensitive; small payload |
| subtotal enterprise       |       |              |                 | 80980              |       |

Table 2 — eu-west-1 baseline (peak hour)
| route_id                   | tier  | baseline_RPS | p95_tok_per_req | baseline_tok_per_s | notes |
|---------------------------|-------|--------------|-----------------|--------------------|-------|
| chat_enterprise_general   | Ent   | 6.5          | 1600            | 10400              | lower volume; similar shape |
| chat_enterprise_longctx   | Ent   | 1.0          | 5900            | 5900               |      |
| embeddings_enterprise     | Ent   | 20.0         | 400             | 8000               |      |
| rerank_enterprise         | Ent   | 7.0          | 850             | 5950               |      |
| subtotal enterprise       |       |              |                 | 30250              |       |

Table 3 — self-serve (aggregate, not per-route; used for overload sharing)
| region     | tier      | peak_RPS | est_tok_per_req(p95) | peak_tok_per_s | notes |
|-----------|-----------|----------|-----------------------|----------------|------|
| us-east-1 | self-serve| 210      | 950                   | 199500         | dominated by chat; mixed models |
| eu-west-1 | self-serve| 95       | 900                   | 85500          |      |

================================================================================
TAB: Forecast — 6 week outlook (planning)

Method:
- Short horizon: simple growth factors per route based on last 4w slope + known customer events (launches, onboarding).
- Add “event bumps” (batch jobs / product launches) as separate line items rather than blending into baseline.

Growth assumptions (weekly compounding, enterprise only):
- chat_enterprise_general: +6%/wk (one large account ramp + general growth)
- chat_enterprise_longctx: +10%/wk (new doc QA use case)
- embeddings_enterprise: +4%/wk (stable)
- rerank_enterprise: +5%/wk

Table 4 — forecasted enterprise tok/s by region (peak hour)
| week_start  | region     | enterprise_tok_per_s (baseline) | comment |
|------------|------------|----------------------------------|---------|
| 2025-02-03 | us-east-1   | 80980                            | baseline week |
| 2025-02-10 | us-east-1   | 85900                            | growth |
| 2025-02-17 | us-east-1   | 91500                            | growth |
| 2025-02-24 | us-east-1   | 97700                            | growth |
| 2025-03-03 | us-east-1   | 104300                           | growth |
| 2025-03-10 | us-east-1   | 111700                           | growth |
| 2025-02-03 | eu-west-1   | 30250                            | baseline week |
| 2025-02-10 | eu-west-1   | 32100                            | growth |
| 2025-02-17 | eu-west-1   | 34200                            | growth |
| 2025-02-24 | eu-west-1   | 36500                            | growth |
| 2025-03-03 | eu-west-1   | 39000                            | growth |
| 2025-03-10 | eu-west-1   | 41800                            | growth |

Event bumps (known-ish; not included in table above):
- One enterprise account “quarterly report generation” batch: +8k tok/s for 60 minutes, ~2x/month (us-east-1).
- Possible migration of one EU customer from hosted to dedicated (would *remove* some EU enterprise lane demand; TBD w/ Lauren).

================================================================================
TAB: Capacity model — effective tok/s supply (planning numbers)

We need a crude mapping from GPU fleet to effective decode tok/s at target latency.

Current planning capacity (effective tok/s) for relevant model classes (per region):
- chat 70B-class pool (includes longctx profile):
  - us-east-1: 155k tok/s effective
  - eu-west-1: 70k tok/s effective
- embeddings/rerank pool:
  - us-east-1: 120k tok/s effective
  - eu-west-1: 55k tok/s effective

Notes:
- “Effective” already assumes typical batching settings + routing distribution and excludes ~8% overhead (maintenance, noisy neighbors, etc.).
- This is not the raw theoretical max and will drift with kernel/runtime changes.

Health/headroom policy (baseline):
- Desired steady-state utilization cap: 70% at peak (=> 30% buffer to absorb microbursts + node loss without paging).
- Enterprise lane reservation is part of that 30% (we do not want enterprise reservation to push self-serve to 85–90% steady-state).

================================================================================
TAB: Incident scenarios — what buffers keep enterprise safe?

We evaluate enterprise lane demand (forecast) against reduced capacity and retry amplification.

Scenario S0 — Normal peak (no incident)
- Should fit with 70% util cap; if not, infra capacity action required (add GPUs / shift traffic / adjust model mix).

Scenario S1 — Regional capacity dip (-25% capacity), no retry storm
- Cause examples: AZ impairment, node health issues, spot churn.

Scenario S2 — Perf regression (-15% capacity) + mild retry amplification (1.3x) on one hot route
- Cause: kernel regression increases latency -> timeouts -> retries.

Scenario S3 — Route-specific retry storm (1.8x RPS) on chat_enterprise_general for 15 minutes + normal capacity
- Cause: client bug (tight retry loop) or SDK misconfig.

Scenario S4 — Worst credible day: -25% capacity + retry storm (1.8x) on chat_enterprise_general
- This is what the “hot-route protection” program is fundamentally about: contain blast radius and keep enterprise lane up.

--------------------------------------------
S1/S2/S3/S4 calculations (Week of 2025-03-10 forecast)

Week 2025-03-10 enterprise demand (peak hour):
- us-east-1: 111,700 tok/s
- eu-west-1: 41,800 tok/s

A) us-east-1, chat pool
- Supply: 155,000 tok/s (normal)
- Supply under -25%: 116,250 tok/s
- Supply under -15%: 131,750 tok/s

Important: enterprise demand above includes embeddings/rerank; to avoid overfitting we allocate enterprise demand to pools using today’s split.
Current split (us-east-1 enterprise tok/s):
- chat routes (general+longctx): 42,940 tok/s of 80,980 tok/s ~ 53%
- embeddings+rerank: 38,040 tok/s ~ 47%
We keep ~same split for forecasted week.

Projected enterprise demand by pool (us-east-1, 2025-03-10):
- chat pool: 111,700 * 0.53 = 59,201 tok/s
- embed/rerank pool: 111,700 * 0.47 = 52,499 tok/s

B) us-east-1, embed/rerank pool
- Supply: 120,000 tok/s (normal)
- Supply under -25%: 90,000 tok/s
- Supply under -15%: 102,000 tok/s

--------------------------------------------
Results — us-east-1 (enterprise only)

Table 5 — us-east-1 enterprise lane feasibility
| scenario | chat_supply_tok/s | chat_demand_tok/s | chat_headroom | embed_supply_tok/s | embed_demand_tok/s | embed_headroom | pass? |
|---------|--------------------|-------------------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|----------------|------|
| S0      | 155000             | 59201             | 95800         | 120000             | 52499              | 67500          | YES |
| S1      | 116250             | 59201             | 57049         | 90000              | 52499              | 37501          | YES |
| S2      | 131750             | 59201*1.3?        | see note      | 102000             | 52499              | 49501          | likely |
| S3      | 155000             | 59201 + delta     | see note      | 120000             | 52499              | 67500          | YES |
| S4      | 116250             | 59201 + delta     | see note      | 90000              | 52499              | 37501          | depends |

Notes on S2/S3/S4:
- Retry amplification typically affects one route, not all enterprise. We model it as affecting chat_enterprise_general only.
- Week 2025-03-10 projected chat demand breakdown (us-east-1):
  - general: ~60% of chat pool demand => 35,500 tok/s
  - longctx: ~40% => 23,700 tok/s
- In S3/S4, only “general” gets multiplied.

Compute delta for retry storm (1.8x on general route):
- Incremental demand = general_tok/s * (1.8 - 1.0) = 35,500 * 0.8 = 28,400 tok/s
- New chat demand under retry storm = 59,200 + 28,400 = 87,600 tok/s

Now check:
- S3 (normal supply): 155,000 - 87,600 = 67,400 tok/s headroom (enterprise lane OK)
- S4 (-25% supply): 116,250 - 87,600 = 28,650 tok/s headroom (enterprise lane OK, but *much* tighter)

Interpretation (us-east-1):
- Enterprise lane can survive S4 on capacity alone *if* we prevent self-serve from consuming chat pool during incident.
- However, this assumes we can isolate capacity effectively (router lanes) and that prefill saturation doesn’t become dominant at longctx.

--------------------------------------------
Results — eu-west-1 (enterprise only)

Week 2025-03-10 enterprise demand: 41,800 tok/s
Apply same split (approx; EU mix slightly more chat-heavy today, but using 55/45 for safety):
- chat pool demand: 23,000 tok/s
- embed/rerank demand: 18,800 tok/s

EU supply:
- chat pool: 70,000 tok/s (normal); 52,500 tok/s under -25%
- embed/rerank pool: 55,000 tok/s (normal); 41,250 tok/s under -25%

Retry storm delta (assume 1.8x on general route, and general is ~70% of EU chat demand):
- general_tok/s ~ 16,100 tok/s
- incremental = 16,100 * 0.8 = 12,880 tok/s
- new chat demand = 23,000 + 12,880 = 35,880 tok/s

Table 6 — eu-west-1 enterprise lane feasibility (week of 2025-03-10)
| scenario | chat_supply_tok/s | chat_demand_tok/s | chat_headroom | embed_supply_tok/s | embed_demand_tok/s | embed_headroom | pass? |
|---------|--------------------|-------------------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|----------------|------|
| S0      | 70000              | 23000             | 47000         | 55000              | 18800              | 36200          | YES |
| S1      | 52500              | 23000             | 29500         | 41250              | 18800              | 22450          | YES |
| S3      | 70000              | 35880             | 34120         | 55000              | 18800              | 36200          | YES |
| S4      | 52500              | 35880             | 16620         | 41250              | 18800              | 22450          | YES (tight) |

Interpretation (eu-west-1):
- EU looks OK on raw capacity under S4, but headroom becomes narrow; any additional drift (perf regression + longctx) can push to queueing/latency.

================================================================================
TAB: Recommended buffers / reservations (proposal)

Goal: pick an enterprise lane reservation per region/pool that is:
- Big enough to cover credible incident combos (S1–S4)
- Small enough not to starve self-serve during normal operation
- Easy to explain and implement in policy engine (config schema)

Recommendation v0 (for review with Mina + SRE):

1) Reserve enterprise lane minimum capacity (per region/pool)
- us-east-1 chat pool: reserve 95k tok/s for enterprise lane during incidents
  - Rationale: covers forecasted enterprise chat (59k) + retry storm delta (28k) + small drift (~8k)
- us-east-1 embed/rerank pool: reserve 70k tok/s
  - Rationale: enterprise demand ~52k + drift/batch bump
- eu-west-1 chat pool: reserve 45k tok/s
- eu-west-1 embed/rerank pool: reserve 30k tok/s

2) “Incident mode” trigger thresholds (when to enforce reservation aggressively)
- If runtime backpressure signal indicates sustained saturation (queue depth > threshold OR p99 > threshold) for 2 min AND enterprise lane error budget burn > 2x, then:
  - Clamp self-serve concurrency / admit rate (shed lower tiers)
  - Keep enterprise admit rate up to reservation ceiling

3) Separate guardrail: max enterprise lane burst (to avoid runaway enterprise client taking whole pool)
- Even enterprise gets bounded (but much higher) burst caps per route.
- Proposed: enterprise route burst cap = 2.2x baseline_RPS for 10 minutes, then back to 1.5x.
  - Needs product/SLA review (Lauren/Nikhil) because this is a behavioral change.

================================================================================
TAB: Sensitivity checks (what breaks the plan?)

1) Long context prefill saturation dominates
- If prefill becomes the bottleneck (not decode tok/s), our tok/s capacity model overestimates ability to absorb spikes.
- Action: get runtime to provide separate prefill_saturation vs decode_saturation signals (ENG-4825), then re-run sizing using whichever dominates.

2) Retry storm amplification > 1.8x
- Some clients do tight loops; we’ve seen >3x in other incidents (not always enterprise).
- Mitigation is primarily admission control + consistent 429 semantics (Retry-After) + support outreach.
- We should model 3.0x as “black swan” and ensure it degrades self-serve, not enterprise.

3) Config propagation delays between regions
- If one region clamps and the other doesn’t, we can create cross-region spillover and oscillation.
- Need: policy versioning + “effective_at” semantics + observability (config age) in dashboards.

4) Self-serve baseline grows faster than assumed
- If self-serve pushes steady-state utilization above 70%, reservation will feel like we’re constantly throttling.
- Infra action: add capacity or reduce default limits; product action: align on expected behavior.

================================================================================
TAB: Open questions / TODOs

- TODO: confirm final “top enterprise routes” list + baseline numbers with PM-612 (Nikhil/Lauren).
- TODO: replace crude tok/s mapping with runtime-provided capacity estimate per model profile (Sofia’s team).
- TODO: align reservation numbers with router’s fairness model (bounded starvation vs strict priority) — see ADR-0147 discussion.
- TODO: decide whether reservations are per-model or per-route+pool (cardinality vs correctness).
- TODO: define explicit rollback thresholds if reservation causes unexpected enterprise latency (counterintuitive, but possible via queue coupling).

================================================================================
Notes / context from incidents (why this sheet exists)

- Near-miss: regional capacity dip where self-serve burst + retries caused elevated tail lat for enterprise chat. Enterprise traffic wasn’t prioritized consistently; some requests queued behind self-serve.
- Postmortem action: quantify reserved capacity needed so we can safely clamp self-serve while staying honest about enterprise behavior.

If you’re editing numbers:
- Please leave a comment line with date + your name + why (e.g., “updated EU baseline due to new customer ramp”).

Change log
